title: Jackson Avenue townhouse development approved after debate
subtitle: Communitech partnership, lower natural gas rate, Rosenberg community centre budget, affordable housing pilot, net-zero climate plan and Habitat for Humanity land donation.
overview: Council approved an Official Plan amendment and rezoning for a stacked townhouse development at 135-161 Jackson Avenue and 136 Brentwood Avenue {{vote:m1}}. The approval came with changes made after the earlier committee meeting, including a lower maximum building height of 11.5 metres written into the planning instruments. Several councillors said they had concerns about density, basement units and the loss of existing rental homes, but weighed those against staff advice and the risk of a worse outcome at the Ontario Land Tribunal.

Council also adopted committee reports that cut the natural gas supply rate for Kitchener Utilities customers from May 1, committed funding to a Communitech partnership, and set the Rosenberg-area community centre budget and name. It approved a pilot incentive for not-for-profit affordable rental and co-op housing, and endorsed a 2050 corporate net-zero target.

In closed session, Council authorized the donation of severed City land at 1035 Ottawa Street North to Habitat for Humanity Waterloo Region for affordable housing, and approved other land and legal matters. Council also approved a tax write-off list and delegated routine property tax adjustments to staff.

decisions.item: Jackson Avenue and Brentwood Avenue development
decisions.detail: Council adopted the Official Plan amendment and approved the rezoning as amended, with a reduced building height, and directed that the urban design brief be applied at site plan approval {{vote:m1}}.
The supply component of the natural gas rate for Kitchener Utilities system gas customers drops from 16.70 to 11.63 cents per cubic metre on May 1, 2024, with quarterly reviews.
Council approved a partnership agreement with Communitech, including $500,000 each in 2024 and 2025 from the Economic Development Investment Fund 2.0, with possible funding in 2026 and 2027.

decisions.item: Affordable rental and co-op housing pilot
decisions.detail: Council approved a new policy and reserve funding for an incentive pilot for not-for-profit affordable rental and co-operative housing, with financial viability checks and a possible mentorship program.

Council approved a total budget of $8,125,000, funded fully from development charges, for the new community centre built jointly with the Catholic school board, and named it The Williamsburg Community Centre.
Council endorsed a corporate 2050 net-zero target and the CorCAP 2.0 Pivot plan, and approved submitting it to the Partners for Climate Protection Program.

decisions.item: Land donation to Habitat for Humanity
decisions.detail: Council authorized the CAO to sever and declare surplus part of 1035 Ottawa Street North and donate it to Habitat for Humanity Waterloo Region for affordable housing.
Staff were directed to implement the proposed traffic calming plan for Dumfries Avenue.

debate: Delegates opposed to the Jackson Avenue project said it was not compatible with the established neighbourhood, that many townhouses were already for sale, and that the site had too little green space, parking and amenity area. One delegate also questioned why the Brentwood Avenue laneway was needed for servicing and fire access.

The applicant's planner said the changes since committee included a one-metre height reduction, a gated emergency-only access and a rental replacement plan for existing tenants. Staff said the fire department requires the second access and that the reduced height would be secured in the zoning by-law.

Some councillors opposed the project over density on a small site, the displacement of tenants, and the lack of affordable or accessible units. One said the rental replacement plan fell short. One said the site had been rezoned recently and the plan should be respected.

Supporters said staff supported the project on planning and provincial policy grounds. They said an appeal to the Ontario Land Tribunal would likely favour the developer and could erase the concessions won. Several still said they disliked the basement units.
Sustainable Waterloo Region's annual update prompted questions about microforests, memorial trees, community gardens, embodied carbon and balancing green space with development.
